svg.aria-label: Diagram: the two-stage sampling pipeline in VPC Flow Logs, where a primary sampling rate varies with host load and cannot be controlled or adjusted, and only the secondary rate applied afterwards is configurable; the pipeline order of filtering, aggregation, secondary sampling, metadata and write to Logging; the asymmetry where egress packets are sampled before egress firewall rules so denied outbound traffic is still visible while ingress packets are sampled after ingress rules so denied inbound traffic is not; the secondary sampling default that differs between the Compute Engine API at fifty percent and the Network Management API at one hundred percent; and the cost, where flow logs are vended network logs billed twice with no free allotment and the aggregation interval is the strongest volume lever
svg.title: VPC Flow Logs: two sampling stages of which you control one, an asymmetric view of blocked traffic, and two charges
svg.text: There are two sampling stages here, and the one people tune is the second one.
The first is set by host load, cannot be adjusted, and decides what the second ever sees.
Stage one: the primary sampling rate, which is not yours
It is DYNAMIC, and varies with the load of the physical host running the reporting resource
at the time of sampling. You CANNOT control it or adjust it.
The probability of sampling a connection RISES WITH ITS PACKET VOLUME, so quiet flows are
the ones most likely to be missed entirely.
Flow logs do not capture every packet. Totals are ESTIMATED from the samples, with an
allowance for what was missed — so bytes and packets are inferences, not counts.
Stage two: the pipeline you do configure, in this order
1. FILTER — generate only matching logs. Expression limit 2,048 characters.
2. AGGREGATE — one entry per 5-tuple per interval: 5s default, up to 15 minutes.
3. SECONDARY SAMPLE — keep a configurable fraction of the entries stage one produced.
4. METADATA — keep all, keep some, or discard every annotation.
5. WRITE to Cloud Logging. Retained 30 days by default.
Secondary sampling of 100% means all of stage one’s output — never all of your traffic.
The default depends on which API built the configuration
COMPUTE ENGINE API: 50% of log entries are kept by default.
NETWORK MANAGEMENT API: 100% of log entries are kept by default.
Same subnet, same intent, two different retention rates and two different bills, decided by
the tool. #73 found the same shape in firewall policy defaults.
Where it sits relative to the firewall, and why that is asymmetric
EGRESS packets are sampled BEFORE egress firewall rules. A denied outbound packet can
still appear in flow logs.
INGRESS packets are sampled AFTER ingress firewall rules. A denied inbound packet is
never sampled at all.
So for blocked INBOUND traffic only #76’s firewall logs can see it. The two instruments
are complements, not alternatives.
What it sees that firewall logs cannot, and what it costs
PROTOCOLS: TCP, UDP, ICMP, ESP, GRE and RDMA — against TCP and UDP only for firewall logs.
Optional TCP CONNECTION LOGGING catches the short-lived flows sampling misses, capped at
100 connections per vCPU per second and 800 per second per VM — the #76 ceiling again.
COST: vended network logs, billed twice, and the 50 GiB free allotment does not apply.
Excluding them from Cloud Logging still leaves the generation charge.
The strongest lever is the AGGREGATION INTERVAL: 5 seconds to 15 minutes is 180 times fewer
intervals, and unlike sampling it loses resolution rather than whole flows.
